scenes.title: Idea to Value
scenes.say: How an idea written in an issue becomes a reviewed, tested change, with people deciding only where it matters.

scenes.title: A factory, for software
scenes.define: A written pipeline that every piece of work follows. Agents do each stage the same way every time, scripts check the result, and people approve at the gates.
scenes.explain: A software factory is a written pipeline that every piece of work follows. Agents do each stage the same way every time, scripts check the result, and people approve at the gates. It turns “ask an assistant to write some code” into a process you can repeat, inspect and trust.
scenes.voice: A software factory is a written pipeline for every piece of work. Agents do the stages, scripts check the results, and people approve at the gates.

scenes.title: Six words to know
points: The stages a piece of work passes through, in order.
One job. Done by an agent, or by a script.
How a job is done, written down once.
Where the work waits for a person to approve.
Proof a section passed, written by a checker.
Picks up new work and keeps it moving.
scenes.explain: Six words describe the whole thing.
scenes.voice: Six words. Pipeline: the stages work goes through. Stage: one job. Skill: how it's done. Gate: a person approves. Evidence: proof it passed. Background job: keeps work moving.

scenes.title: One factory, many repositories
points: One editor and one background job, on one machine.
As many as you like. This demo uses two: an API and a UI.
Each repository has one or more: features, bugs, reviewing pull requests.
scenes.explain: There is one factory: one editor and one background job. It serves as many repositories as you like, and each repository has one or more pipelines, such as one for features, a shorter one for bugs, and one that reviews pull requests. This demo runs five pipelines across two repositories. One limit to know: a single pipeline works on one repository, so an idea that spans two is two issues today.
scenes.voice: One factory serves many repositories. Each repository can have several pipelines: one for features, a shorter one for bugs, one for reviews.

scenes.title: A maker builds, a checker proves
scenes.say: Two separate sessions for every section. Then a script checks them both.
scenes.explain: Every task names the skill that builds it. The factory starts a maker session, which builds one section and may not tick anything or write evidence. It then starts a checker in a different session, which never saw the maker work: it runs the section's gate against what was built, writes the evidence, and ticks the tasks only if everything passed. The factory rejects a maker that ticks its own work and a checker that edits code, and it stamps each evidence file with both session ids. In this run four sections were each built in one session and proved in another, eight sessions in all, using the logic, view, page and tests skills.
scenes.voice: Now, a maker builds, and a checker proves.

scenes.title: Other pipelines, same factory
scenes.say: A bug needs a shorter pipeline. An API change needs a stricter one.
scenes.explain: The same factory runs other pipelines at the same time. On the API repository, feature work has two gates before any code, because API changes are costly to undo. Bugs take a short pipeline with no spec: reproduce with a failing test, fix, review, then one gate. A bug filed in this demo went from issue to a reviewed fix in under three minutes.

scenes.title: No process, no review
scenes.say: Every pull request is checked by a script first. Only work that followed the process earns an agent's time.
scenes.explain: A review pipeline checks pull requests, whoever wrote them. A script goes first: is there a spec, does every task name a skill, is there evidence, did the tests change with the code, plus the team's own rules. A quick hack added by hand was stopped by the script and cost nothing. The request the factory built passed all 11 checks, and only then did an agent review the code.
